MOS is a name where the quant and qual axes are sending different signals that deserve attention. The quant side scores green, but this is generous — Debt/EV at ~40% is firmly in the yellow zone for an IG fertilizer name, and the red maturity flag ($863M due 2026 with the revolver already drawn $570M against zero disclosed capacity) creates real near-term refinancing risk that the green composite arguably understates. Interest coverage at 13.4x is comfortable, but the trajectory is deteriorating: net debt jumped $829M in 2025 on a massive $960M working capital drag, the $900M November 2025 note raise was redirected from refinancing the 2027 wall to merely retiring CP, and management explicitly signaled leverage is increasing with shareholder returns subordinated to deleveraging. The qual side correctly flags elevated risk (tariff exposure on Canadian potash, sulfur cost headwinds compressing H1 margins by ~$250M, $1.5B capex year, environmental liabilities on Florida phosphogypsum stacks) and cautious tone, but a single red on risk with everything else yellow feels light given the cumulative weight of headwinds.

**Desk summary:** MOS matters right now because the 2026 maturity wall ($863M) lands into a year of compressed margins from sulfur cost spikes, elevated capex ($1.5B), and a balance sheet that just absorbed an $829M net debt increase — with the revolver already drawn and management having burned the November note proceeds on CP retirement rather than pre-funding the 2027 maturity. Watch the H1 2026 working capital release ($300-500M guided) and phosphate production ramp toward 7Mt as the key tests of whether free cash flow materializes above the dividend; if the working capital unwind disappoints or potash tariff risk re-escalates, the 2026/2027 maturity stack becomes a real liquidity event for an IG-rated name trading at 40% Debt/EV with pricing power clearly pressured.

Moss Creek Resources is a private Permian Basin (Midland Basin) oil-weighted E&P operating as a subsidiary of Surge Energy US Holdings. The company executed a smart refinancing in Aug 2024: issued $750M 8.25% Senior Unsecured Notes due 2031 and used proceeds to retire both the $500M 7.50% 2026 notes and $499M 10.50% 2027 notes, reducing total bond debt by ~$249M and saving ~$25M annually in interest expense. The 8.25% coupon on the 2031 notes reflects B+/B+ rating (S&P/Fitch) -- solid single-B private E&P. An RBL facility is in place (KeyBank-led) but drawn balance and terms are not publicly disclosed. The Midland Basin is one of the most prolific oil basins in the US, providing favorable well economics at WTI above $50. As a private operator under Surge Energy, financial disclosure is limited. Leverage and production metrics are available only from the offering memorandum. The 2031 maturity provides 5+ years of runway with no refinancing pressure. No maintenance covenants on the unsecured notes. The credit question is whether the Surge Energy/Moss Creek platform can sustain the $750M debt load through a commodity downturn -- the Aug 2024 refinancing was credit-positive (reduced total debt, cut interest expense, extended maturity by 5 years), suggesting competent balance sheet management. Bull catalyst: Midland Basin well results outperforming + oil above $80 generating FCF for deleveraging + potential Surge Energy IPO or strategic sale. Bear catalyst: oil below $50 compressing Midland Basin economics + Surge platform acquisitions adding leverage before existing debt is reduced. The Aug 2024 refinancing is the most credit-positive recent action in the file.

Matador Resources is a Permian Basin (Delaware Basin) oil-weighted E&P that has grown aggressively through a combination of organic drilling and the $1.9B Ameredev acquisition (2024). LTM financials: revenue $3.70B, EBITDA $2.44B, operating cash flow $2.43B against LTM interest expense of $209M. Capital structure: $3.55B total debt ($3.40B long-term), $79M cash, producing net debt of $3.47B and leverage of 1.4x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is comfortable at 11.7x. The debt stack was completely reshaped in early 2026: the 5.875% 2026 notes and 6.875% 2028 notes (~84% tendered Mar 2026) are effectively retired, replaced by $900M 6.50% Senior Notes due 2032 and $750M 6.00% Senior Notes due 2034. This pushes the nearest bond maturity to 2032 -- one of the cleanest maturity profiles in Permian E&P. The $3.25B RBL ($2.25B elected commitment, ~$398M drawn at YE2025) matures 2029. LTM capex of $2.18B produces negative LTM FCF of $242M, reflecting the aggressive growth investment phase. The credit question is whether Matador's growth capex (spending nearly 90% of operating cash flow) will generate sufficient reserve additions and production growth to bring leverage below 1.0x, or whether the reinvestment rate is too aggressive for a 1.4x levered credit. Bull catalyst: Delaware Basin well results exceeding type curves + oil above $80 driving FCF inflection + maturity profile now clear to 2032. Bear catalyst: oil below $60 making $2.2B capex unsustainable + RBL redetermination risk if reserves underperform + Ameredev integration costs exceeding projections. The early 2026 liability management exercise was excellent -- eliminated all near-term maturities and reduced weighted-average coupon.

MTW sits at the intersection of improving momentum and genuine structural concern. The fundamental score is weak in absolute terms (-0.11) and bottom-half versus peers (-0.57), but the strong positive momentum (+0.59) is doing the heavy lifting — this is a name getting better from a bad place, not a name that's arrived. The quant/qual divergence here matters: quant lands green on the back of no maturity wall (2031 notes), adequate liquidity ($298M), and momentum, while qual flags red on risk severity driven by escalating tariffs on steel/aluminum derivatives, the $45.6M EPA cash drain, a loss-making EURAF segment (-$42.9M operating loss on $667M revenue), and rising total debt (+18% YoY to $461M). Debt/EV at 58% is in the yellow band and tells the real story better than the 4.0x gross leverage figure (which includes only ~$7M of EBITDA add-backs, so it's less distorted than many HY names, but still masks the reality that LTM EBITDA of ~$115-122M barely services $42M+ in annual cash interest — coverage at 2.9x is thin and deteriorating). The $144.6M revolver draw (up from $79M) against a $325M facility is a liquidity trend heading the wrong direction even as total liquidity looks okay on paper.

**Desk summary:** MTW is a cautious hold — the scoring composite yellow is fair, but the green quant axis is flattering a name whose 2.9x interest coverage, 58% Debt/EV, and rising revolver reliance leave minimal margin for error if tariff mitigation slips below the ~85% offset management claims or if EURAF losses persist. Watch Q1 2026 FCF conversion against the $40-65M full-year guide closely: if the EPA settlement was truly one-time and backlog ($794M, +22%) converts at guided margins, deleveraging below 3.0x net is achievable and the 9.25% 2031 second liens look money-good; if flat rental rates, tariff escalation, or European weakness stall the trajectory, this credit gets ugly fast given the thin coverage cushion.

MTX is a red-red composite where the axes agree but for somewhat different reasons, and the springing maturity trigger is the single most important near-term issue. The $398M of 5.0% Senior Notes due January 2028 have not been refinanced, which means both the $400M revolver and the $563M term loan spring to an October 2027 maturity — barely 18 months away — collapsing MTX's entire $1B+ capital structure into a compressed window. Debt/EV at ~36% is genuinely comfortable and suggests the market is not pricing existential credit stress, but that metric becomes irrelevant if the company cannot access the revolver or faces a technical default on the term loan due to the springing trigger. Management on the Q4 call did not discuss refinancing at all, which is a notable omission given the timeline pressure — they need to take out or refi >$348M of the unsecured notes (down to the $50M carve-out) before October 2027 to avoid the spring.

The fundamental score is negative and deteriorating versus specialty chemical peers, driven by the $215M talc accrual crushing GAAP EBITDA to ~$146M (adjusted EBITDA is $368M once you strip litigation charges). Interest coverage at 6.8x on adjusted numbers is adequate, and net leverage on management's adjusted basis at ~1.7x provides substantial covenant headroom against the 4.0x test. But the talc liability is genuinely open-ended — management calls reserves "sufficient" but the filing explicitly warns ultimate costs could materially exceed the accrual, and the Pfizer indemnity scope remains unresolved. The cautious management tone, lack of refinancing discussion, and FCF that disappointed analysts in 2025 all point to a management team that may be running behind on addressing the maturity wall.

**Desk summary:** MTX's primary credit event is the springing maturity on the revolver and term loan triggered by the unaddressed $398M of 2028 unsecured notes — management's silence on refinancing plans with only ~18 months to the October 2027 spring date is the single biggest red flag, especially with an unresolved talc liability that could complicate market access. Murphy Oil is a diversified E&P with oil-weighted production of ~180-190k boepd split between the Eagle Ford Shale (onshore Texas) and the Gulf of Mexico (deepwater). LTM financials: revenue $2.72B, EBITDA $1.25B, operating cash flow $1.25B, FCF $198M. Capital structure: $2.20B total debt ($1.38B long-term), $377M cash, producing net debt of $1.83B and leverage of 1.5x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is solid at 13.0x on $96M LTM interest expense. The debt stack was completely overhauled: all legacy 2027/2028/2029 notes were retired in 2024-2026, replaced by $600M 6.0% Senior Notes due 2032 and $500M 6.5% Senior Notes due 2034. The $2.0B senior unsecured revolving credit facility (upsized from $1.35B, maturity extended to 2031) is fully undrawn -- Murphy funds operations entirely from cash flow. Weighted-average coupon is ~6.1% with weighted-average maturity of ~8.3 years. No near-term maturities before 2032. No maintenance covenants on the unsecured notes. The credit question is whether Murphy can sustain its dual-basin model (Eagle Ford + GOM deepwater) at scale with only $198M LTM FCF after $1.05B capex -- the FCF yield is thin relative to the $2.2B debt load, and GOM deepwater projects carry lumpy execution risk. Bull catalyst: GOM deepwater development success (King's Quay, Samurai, Mormont wells) + Eagle Ford well cost deflation + oil above $80 expanding FCF significantly. Bear catalyst: GOM drilling disappointment + oil below $60 compressing EBITDA toward $800M and raising leverage above 2.5x + deepwater maintenance capex surprise. The clean maturity profile to 2032 and undrawn $2.0B revolver provide substantial liquidity cushion.

MWA (Mueller Water Products) — Desk Summary

The green-red axis divergence here is a narrative problem, not a numbers problem. The quantitative picture is pristine: Debt/EV at ~10.5% is deeply investment-grade territory, the single $450mm unsecured note doesn't mature until June 2029 with a springing ABL 91 days prior, interest coverage at 20.5x is exceptional, and total liquidity of ~$595mm (including $460mm cash) against zero revolver draws leaves no near-term stress. Fundamental score is strong (0.71 peer-relative) with positive momentum, reflecting record EBITDA margins and robust free cash flow conversion.

The qualitative red flags — elevated risk severity and capital allocation concern — are real but appropriately weighted for equity/strategic risk rather than credit risk. The step-up in capex to 4–5% of net sales (from ~3%) for domestic foundry expansion, a simultaneous CEO and CFO transition within 12 months, geopolitical exposure at the Krausz Israel facility, tariff headwinds on imported components, and 37% revenue concentration in two distributors with no long-term contracts all matter directionally but are buffered by a balance sheet carrying nearly as much cash as total debt. The allocation score flagging "policy change" reflects the capex acceleration and increasing buybacks/dividends, which modestly tilt the cash flow waterfall away from bondholders but from such a low-leverage starting point that it barely registers as credit-negative.

**What matters now:** This is a name where the bonds should trade tight and stay tight unless the capex program balloons, M&A appetite turns aggressive with leverage, or the 2029 refi window coincides with a meaningful deterioration in municipal spending. Watch for (1) any acquisition announcement that meaningfully adds debt — management signaled "open to" M&A with no stated leverage target, which is the real allocation risk; (2) the cadence of the capex ramp and whether FCF conversion holds above 80% of adjusted net income; and (3) residential construction weakness spreading into municipal budgets, which would compress volumes into the elevated fixed-cost base from the foundry investments. The composite yellow feels right — the credit is clean today, but the qualitative flags correctly identify

Nabors Industries is one of the world's largest land drilling companies, operating approximately 350 rigs in the US, Saudi Arabia (via the SANAD joint venture with Saudi Aramco), and other international markets. LTM financials: revenue $3.19B, EBITDA $1.31B, FCF -$23M against $215M LTM interest expense. Capital structure: $2.57B total debt, $941M cash, producing net debt of $1.63B and leverage of 1.2x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 6.1x. The bond stack was aggressively reshaped in 2024-2026: the 7.375% 2027 and 7.50% 2028 notes were both redeemed, replaced by $650M 9.125% Senior Priority Guaranteed Notes due 2030, $550M 8.875% Senior Guaranteed Notes due 2031, and $700M 7.625% Senior Priority Guaranteed Notes due 2032 (newest, Nov 2025). Total bonded debt is ~$1.9B with no maturity before 2029. The guarantee structure creates a tiered priority: Senior Priority Guaranteed claims rank above Senior Guaranteed. $941M cash position provides significant optionality. The credit question is whether Nabors can sustain the Saudi SANAD partnership revenue while managing the US land rig count cyclicality, or whether the $2.6B total debt load (even at 1.2x leverage) constrains the credit in a prolonged US activity downturn. Bull catalyst: Saudi Arabia increasing SANAD rig count + US land drilling recovery + deleveraging below 1.0x. Bear catalyst: US rig count decline + Saudi activity plateau + 9%+ coupons creating heavy interest burden ($215M). The SANAD JV with Saudi Aramco provides unique revenue visibility through the Saudi relationship.

Nordson (NDSN) is a well-positioned IG industrial name where the quant and qual axes are slightly divergent but not alarming. The quant side scores green on the back of strong peer-relative fundamentals (65th percentile), a benign 12% Debt/EV, robust liquidity (~$945M revolver availability plus $120M cash against only $54M maturing in 2026), and 7.7x interest coverage — the maturity wall red flag is mechanical noise given the 2026 current portion is a trivially small $54M against ample liquidity. The qual side scores yellow because the risk assessment flags genuine elevated macro/tariff exposure for a company generating 67% of revenue internationally, and capital allocation is aggressive for a deleveraging story: $86M in buybacks plus $46M in dividends in Q1 FY2026 alone means shareholder returns are consuming the majority of free cash flow, which constrains the pace of debt paydown even as management touts a 2.0x–2.5x leverage target and ended fiscal 2025 at 2.1x.

The real watch item is the tariff/trade policy risk intersecting with the ATS segment's cyclical semiconductor exposure — ATS posted 20.7% organic growth in Q1 FY2026, but this is a segment that can reverse sharply, and China-sourced input costs face direct tariff pressure that management has not explicitly addressed on hedging or pass-through. Management tone is genuinely confident with raised guidance and record FCF conversion (136% in FY2025), so the narrative is strong, but the scoring correctly flags that if tariff headwinds materialize alongside an ATS demand reversal, the current shareholder-return-heavy allocation leaves less cushion than the balance sheet optically suggests. The composite yellow feels right — this is not a credit stress story but a "watch the macro" story where the next two quarters of margin trajectory and any trade policy escalation will determine whether this stays comfortably IG or faces ratings pressure. Watch IPS margin recovery (down 380bps in Q1 on mix), ATS order sustainability, and whether management pulls back buybacks if tariff costs accelerate.

Noble Finance II is the bond-issuing entity for Noble Corporation, the world's second-largest offshore drilling contractor by fleet size (after Transocean). Noble operates a fleet of jackup and floating rigs serving IOCs and NOCs globally. LTM financials (consolidated Noble Corp): revenue $3.29B, EBITDA $1.10B, FCF $432M against $162M LTM interest expense. Capital structure: ~$1.98B total debt (all long-term), $471M cash, producing net debt of $1.50B and leverage of 1.4x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 6.8x. The sole unsecured bond tranche is ~$1.475B 8.0% Senior Notes due Apr 2030 (issued across three sub-tranches: $600M Apr 2023 + $675M 2023 tap + $800M Aug 2024 tap). A revolving credit facility provides additional liquidity. DO (Diamond Foreign Asset Co) is a subsidiary of Noble -- DO's $550M 8.50% 2030 secured notes sit at the Diamond Offshore entity level, structurally separate from NEFINA bonds. Combined Noble complex debt (NEFINA + DO) is ~$2.5B. The credit question is whether Noble's combined fleet (post-Diamond Offshore acquisition) generates sufficient EBITDA to support the ~$2.5B combined debt load through the offshore cycle, particularly as deepwater day rates face potential mean reversion. Bull catalyst: deepwater day rates sustained above $450k/day + contract backlog growth + leverage declining below 1.0x. Bear catalyst: offshore capex pullback + day rate compression from newbuild competition + Diamond integration challenges. NEFINA bonds are unsecured parent-level claims; DO bonds are secured subsidiary-level claims -- structural analysis matters in a stress scenario.

NEU is a well-covered IG specialty chemicals name where the quant picture is clean — 14% Debt/EV, 17.9x interest coverage, fully unsecured stack with no maturities before 2029, strong liquidity, and active deleveraging ($88M debt reduction in 2025 even while funding the Calca acquisition) — yet the qualitative axis drags to yellow on a red risk score driven by elevated environmental liabilities, high customer concentration among a handful of major oil companies, and the secular EV headwind to the core petroleum additives franchise. The divergence here is a narrative problem, not a numbers problem: the fundamentals are solid but the momentum is deteriorating (-0.086) as volume declines of ~5% and pricing pressure in petroleum additives signal the core business is softening, and management's cautious tone on tariffs and inflation with no formal guidance (and notably no live Q&A) doesn't inspire confidence that the trajectory reverses near-term.

What matters right now is whether the ~$1 billion strategic pivot into specialty materials (AMPAC/Calca) — defense-oriented, higher-margin, lower-cyclicality — can offset the structural erosion in petroleum additives before it shows up in the credit metrics. The 2029 maturity ($288M) is comfortable, but watch for continued volume/pricing deterioration in petroleum additives over the next two to three quarters; if LTM EBITDA compresses materially from the current $709M while capex guidance is increasing, the deleveraging story stalls and the green quant score could flip faster than the comfortable Debt/EV suggests. The absence of a live analyst Q&A on the earnings call is an unusual governance signal for a company of this quality — worth flagging but not actionable alone.

NGL Energy Operating is a diversified midstream MLP focused on water solutions (produced water disposal in the Permian and Bakken), crude oil logistics, and NGL marketing. LTM financials: revenue $3.18B, EBITDA $639M, FCF $291M against $259M LTM interest expense. Capital structure: $3.15B total debt, $6M cash, producing net debt of $3.15B and leverage of 4.9x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 2.5x. The Feb 2024 $2.9B refinancing was transformational: $900M 8.125% Senior Secured Notes due Feb 2029 and $1.3B 8.375% Senior Secured Notes due Feb 2032 replaced the prior debt stack, with the 7.50% 2026 notes fully retired. All current bonds are secured, reflecting the prior distress history (NGL was a CCC-rated credit in 2020-2021). The water solutions business is the growth driver and primary EBITDA contributor, benefiting from Permian Basin production growth. The credit question is whether EBITDA growth from the water business can bring leverage below 4x, or whether the 8%+ coupon on $2.2B of secured notes permanently constrains cash flow and prevents deleveraging. Bull catalyst: Permian water volumes growing + EBITDA exceeding $700M + leverage declining below 4x. Bear catalyst: Permian production plateau reducing water volumes + leverage remaining above 5x + secured notes limiting financial flexibility. The Feb 2024 refi was credit-positive -- extended maturities and simplified the stack -- but the secured structure and high coupons reflect the legacy distress history.

Northern Oil and Gas is a unique non-operated E&P holding working interests in ~9,000+ gross wells across the Williston Basin (Bakken) and Permian Basin, plus a growing Appalachian (Utica) position. The non-op model means NOG does not drill wells -- it acquires mineral/working interests and receives proportional production, paying its share of D&C costs. LTM financials: revenue $2.10B, EBITDA $1.05B, operating cash flow $1.51B. Capital structure: $2.40B total debt (all long-term), $14M cash, producing net debt of $2.38B and leverage of 2.3x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 6.1x on $172M LTM interest expense. Negative LTM net income of -$400M and FCF of -$291M reflect aggressive acquisition spending (including $852M in Q4 2025 alone -- likely the Ohio Utica entry). The debt stack is clean post-Mar 2026: the 8.125% 2028 notes (~$20M residual) were fully redeemed, leaving $725M 7.875% Senior Notes due 2033 as the sole bond tranche. The $1.975B RBL ($1.8B elected commitment, maturity Nov 2030) is the primary debt instrument. No near-term bond maturities until 2033 -- 7+ year runway. The credit question is whether the non-op acquisition model can sustain $2.4B of debt through a commodity downturn -- NOG's leverage is structural (the model requires continuous acquisition capex to offset compounding decline rates across thousands of wells), not transient. Bull catalyst: oil above $80 + Utica acquisition delivering volumes + operator-driven well cost deflation reducing NOG's D&C burden. Bear catalyst: oil below $55 + RBL redetermination cutting borrowing base + compounding decline rates outpacing acquisition pace. The 2.3x leverage is the highest among pure oil-weighted names after CRGYFN, and the non-op model's inability to control drilling pace is a unique structural risk.

Northriver Midstream is a private Canadian G&P midstream company operating in the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin (British Columbia), primarily serving Tourmaline Oil Corp and CNRL under long-term acreage dedications. The debt stack was cleanly refinanced in Jul 2024: the $525M 5.625% Senior Secured Notes due 2026 were tendered (~$473M accepted) and replaced by $525M 6.750% Senior Secured Notes due Jul 2032. This was an excellent liability management move -- extended maturity by 6 years and eliminated the imminent 2026 wall. No revolver details are publicly available. Northriver's BC operations primarily involve sour gas gathering and processing, which requires specialized infrastructure and creates high barriers to entry. The Tourmaline/CNRL customer concentration provides volume stability under long-term dedications but also creates single-counterparty risk. The credit question is whether the Tourmaline/CNRL dedications provide sufficient contracted volume to service $525M of secured debt through a WCSB gas price downturn, or whether the private opacity and Canadian-basin exposure cap the credit. Bull catalyst: Tourmaline production growth driving above-MVC volumes + BC gas pricing improvement + potential IPO/strategic sale. Bear catalyst: Tourmaline/CNRL reducing WCSB drilling activity + AECO gas price collapse + Canadian pipeline egress constraints. The 6.75% secured coupon reflects BB-level private midstream quality with Canadian jurisdiction risk.
Limited public data available. Private credit — no SEC filings or market data for scoring.

Insight Enterprises is a conservative IT solutions distributor credit with 1.2x gross leverage, $358MM cash, and a $2B ABL facility providing ample liquidity. The $500MM 6.625% Senior Notes due May 2032 (issued May 2024 to refinance the 0.75% Convertible Notes) represent the sole fixed-rate bond exposure; the ABL ($868MM drawn at Dec 2025, ~5.34% SOFR-based) is the primary working capital tool for a distributor with large swings in accounts receivable from hardware sales. Net earnings declined to $157MM in 2025 from $250MM in 2024 — reflecting margin compression in the hardware distribution business amid vendor pricing dynamics and IT spending normalization post-AI infrastructure surge. Interest coverage of 4.9x on $493MM total debt relative to $417MM EBITDA provides solid debt service cushion. The business model risk is structural — hardware distribution is a low-margin, commoditized market where CDW, SHI, and direct vendor competition are constant. The strategic shift to managed services and solutions (Amdaris, recent acquisitions) is designed to improve margin profile but takes time. ABL covenant compliance (no financial maintenance covenants disclosed on the ABL; event-of-default based) gives operational flexibility.

NuStar Logistics is the bond-issuing subsidiary of NuStar Energy LP, which was acquired by Sunoco LP (SUN) in 2024 for $7.3B. Post-acquisition, NSUS bonds are structurally subordinate to SUN-level debt -- equity signals on SUN US propagate to both SUN and NSUS bond tickers. The legacy NSUS bond stack included $300M 6.0% 2026 notes (fully redeemed Mar 2026 via SUN's $1.2B issuance) and $600M 6.375% Senior Notes due Oct 2030. The 6.375% 2030 notes are the surviving NSUS-level tranche, sitting below SUN's ~$16B consolidated debt. No standalone NSUS financial reporting post-merger -- all metrics are consolidated at SUN level. At SUN level: LTM EBITDA $1.81B, total debt $16.1B, leverage 8.4x, interest coverage 3.3x. The NSUS bonds are effectively claims on SUN's pipeline and terminal assets, which are among the highest-quality infrastructure assets in the Sunoco portfolio. The credit question is whether the structural subordination of NSUS bonds to SUN-level debt creates meaningful recovery risk in a stress scenario, or whether the infrastructure asset quality provides adequate protection. Bull catalyst: SUN deleveraging improving coverage for all subsidiaries + NSUS-level asset performance. Bear catalyst: SUN credit stress flowing down to NSUS + gasoline demand decline reducing pipeline utilization. The Mar 2026 redemption of the 6.0% 2026 notes at SUN level was a positive signal -- the parent is actively managing subsidiary maturities.

Nutrien screens as a comfortable IG credit with Debt/EV at ~27%, well inside the 35% green threshold for commodity chemicals, and interest coverage at 8.9x provides substantial cushion even if fertilizer prices soften. The one flag worth watching is the **red maturity score**: ~$1.7 billion in short-term debt maturing in 2026, which against only $700 million in cash looks tight on a standalone basis — but management already demonstrated willingness to address this, having paid down $600 million in short-term debt during 2025 using FCF and $900 million in divestiture proceeds. With decreasing capex ($2.0-2.1B, well below prior targets), ongoing non-core divestitures (phosphate review, Brazil retail restructuring), and LTM EBITDA above $6 billion, the 2026 wall should be manageable through a combination of refinancing and internal cash generation, though the absence of disclosed revolver capacity in the data is a gap worth confirming.

The quant-qual axes are aligned green, which is appropriate here — this is not a divergence story. The allocation score landing at yellow rather than green reflects the tension between debt reduction and simultaneous buyback increases, but for an IG name generating this level of EBITDA with a deleveraging trajectory, that's a reasonable capital allocation posture, not a credit concern. If anything, the maturity red flag may be slightly overstated given the demonstrated paydown velocity and divestiture pipeline still in progress.

**Desk summary:** Nutrien is a well-covered IG commodity chemical name with Debt/EV at 27% and 8.9x coverage, running a clean deleveraging playbook via divestitures and capex discipline — the only actionable item is the ~$1.7B 2026 maturity wall against limited reported cash, but management's track record of $600M+ paydown last year and ongoing phosphate/Brazil strategic reviews suggest this gets addressed without stress. Watch for refinancing announcements on the short-term tranche and any color on the phosphate review timeline, as proceeds from those divestitures could front-load the maturity solution and potentially tighten spreads further.

Nufarm (NUF.AX) is a name where the quant and qual axes are sharply divergent, and the answer is timing — the numbers are still deeply stressed but the trajectory is moving in the right direction, and the question is whether the 2026 unsecured maturity wall gets addressed before liquidity becomes existential.

**The core problem is the A$620M senior unsecured notes due 2026 against a market cap of only ~A$877M and Debt/EV of 76%.** This is not a leverage ratio story — the GAAP interest coverage at 0.79x tells you EBITDA doesn't even cover interest, and the 8.4x gross leverage is distorted by depressed LTM EBITDA that includes the trough. But Debt/EV at 76% is unambiguous: the equity cushion beneath the debt stack is dangerously thin, and a missed refinancing window on the 2026s would be a capital structure event. Liquidity is technically adequate today (A$475M cash plus A$335M undrawn revolver), but the 2026 maturity consumes more than the entire cash balance, and the revolver itself matures in 2027, so there's no bridge without new capital market access.

**The qualitative side is genuinely constructive.** Management claimed A$538M of net debt reduction in H2 FY25, guided capex below A$200M, and is targeting 2.0x leverage by end of FY26 — implying roughly A$400M+ of further net debt reduction from EBITDA recovery and working capital discipline. Crop Protection EBITDA grew 18% with margin expansion across all regions, the new CEO is signaling cost discipline as a cultural shift, and Seed Technologies is being right-sized to self-fund. Tone is confident, guidance was raised, and the fundamental momentum score (0.682) confirms improving peer-relative trends. The transcript's refinancing language ("no near-term need") is notable but arguably contradicted by the 2026 maturity sitting right on top of them.

**The scoring flags are directionally correct but the composite red is primarily a maturity-wall and Debt/EV call, not a deteriorating operations call.**

NVRI is a binary credit story hinging entirely on the Clean Earth/Veolia sale closing mid-2026: the current consolidated entity carries $1.8B of debt against only $171M GAAP LTM EBITDA (management-adjusted to ~$345M via large add-backs including $30M+ Rail forward loss provisions and impairments), with Debt/EV at 54% — not yet crisis territory but moving the wrong direction as the fundamental score is deep red at -1.0 with sharply negative momentum (-1.39), meaning NVRI is deteriorating faster than peers across leverage, coverage, and cash flow metrics. The axes diverge meaningfully — quant lands yellow only because Debt/EV hasn't breached 70% and the nearest hard maturity ($475M unsecured notes) is 2028, while qual is red on legitimate grounds: Rail ETO contracts are burning ~$40M/year cash with vendor bankruptcy risk, covenant headroom is razor-thin (4.93x vs 5.25x cap, requiring a November 2025 amendment after projected non-compliance), liquidity is tight with $526M of $675M revolver drawn and only $104M cash, and management now signals New Enviri may need to retain more sale proceeds than expected to backstop Rail — directly pressuring bondholder recoveries.

**What to watch:** The singular catalyst is the Veolia close (August 2026 deadline, extendable to November); if it fails, the $80M termination fee plus stranded costs land on a balance sheet with 2.79x interest coverage, a nearly maxed revolver, and a covenant structure that already required emergency amendment — that's a liquidity crisis scenario. Even if it closes, pro forma New Enviri at ~$140M EBITDA with breakeven FCF and residual Rail execution risk will need a clean refinancing of whatever debt remains, and the 5.75% senior unsecured notes due 2028 become the fulcrum instrument depending on how much debt survives the separation. The composite yellow feels generous — this is a deal-contingent credit where the downside absent closing is red across every dimension.

Bull catalyst: deepwater ROV demand growth + fleet expansion at attractive returns + potential IG upgrade or full debt retirement. PBF Holding is an independent petroleum refiner operating 6 refineries with ~1 million bpd throughput capacity across the East Coast (Delaware City, Paulsboro), Gulf Coast (Chalmette), Mid-Continent (Toledo), and West Coast (Torrance, Martinez). LTM financials: revenue $29.3B, EBITDA $107M (trough refining margins), operating cash flow -$78M, FCF -$783M. Capital structure: $2.90B total debt ($2.15B long-term), $528M cash, producing net debt of $2.37B. Leverage is effectively unquantifiable at $107M EBITDA -- in a normal crack spread environment ($20-25 3-2-1), PBF generates $2-3B EBITDA. The bond stack consists of $1.0B 6.0% Senior Notes due Feb 2028, $500M 7.875% Notes due Sep 2030, and $800M 9.875% Notes due 2030 (issued Mar 2025). Interest coverage at trough is 0.6x -- the company is burning cash. No near-term maturities before Feb 2028. The credit question is entirely about crack spread cyclicality: at $15 3-2-1 cracks (trough), PBF generates barely enough to cover interest; at $25 cracks (mid-cycle), EBITDA jumps to $2B+ and leverage drops below 1.5x. This is the most cyclical credit in energy coverage -- EBITDA can swing $2B+ between peak and trough. Bull catalyst: crack spread recovery above $25 + summer driving season demand + refinery closures tightening capacity. Bear catalyst: sustained sub-$15 cracks + demand destruction from EV adoption + any refinery operational incident (Torrance/Martinez). The $800M 9.875% 2030 notes (Mar 2025) were issued at trough margins -- a signal that PBF needed liquidity insurance during the downturn.

The 2025 issuance of $230MM in 1.5% convertible notes due 2030 adds a new refinancing layer and near-term dilution risk. Overall: legacy secular decline with adequate near-term liquidity but a discrete 2026 refinancing execution risk that must be monitored closely.

Rockcliff Energy II is a private Haynesville Shale natural gas producer acquired by TG Natural Resources (a subsidiary of Tokyo Gas) in 2024 for $2.7B equity / ~$4.6B total enterprise value. The sole public bond tranche is $700M 5.50% Senior Unsecured Notes due Oct 2029, which were assumed by TGNR at closing. As a subsidiary of a Japanese utility, the credit profile has transformed from single-B private E&P to a quasi-investment-grade credit backed by Tokyo Gas (A-rated by JCR). However, bond documentation and covenants remain as originally issued -- the structural protection is only as good as the parent guarantee, which may not be explicit. Production was approximately 1.3 Bcf/d gross operated in the Haynesville at the time of acquisition, making Rockcliff one of the basin's larger operators. Post-acquisition financial disclosure is limited -- TGNR does not provide standalone Rockcliff financials. The 5.50% coupon is the lowest in private gas E&P coverage, reflecting the 2021 issuance vintage when rates were low. The maturity in Oct 2029 provides 3+ years of runway. The credit question is whether Tokyo Gas's strategic commitment to US gas production provides implicit support that makes the 5.50% 2029 notes money-good regardless of standalone economics, or whether Rockcliff could be cut loose in a prolonged gas downturn. Bull catalyst: Tokyo Gas explicit guarantee or support agreement + Henry Hub above $4 validating the acquisition economics. Bear catalyst: Tokyo Gas writing down the $4.6B investment in a gas downturn + TGNR operational restructuring that subordinates Rockcliff bondholders. The 5.50% coupon on 2029 paper with implicit Japanese parent backing is an attractive risk-reward in the HY gas E&P space.

REZI credit profile is in active transformation on two axes: (1) resolution of the Honeywell indemnification obligation via an August 2025 term loan raise of $1.225B that ballooned total debt to $3.23B, and (2) the announced ADI Global Distribution spin-off that will separate the two segments into independent entities. The reported LTM EBITDA of -$126MM is a product of the non-recurring indemnification charge, not reflective of operating performance; underlying Products and Solutions and ADI generate positive and improving EBITDA. With $661MM of cash and a $500MM undrawn revolver (maturing June 2029), near-term liquidity is adequate. The A&R Term B Facility carries three tranches: $518MM maturing February 2028, $591MM maturing June 2031, and $1.222B incremental maturing August 2032, plus $300MM 4.0% Notes (2029) and $600MM 6.5% Notes (2032). Critical risk for bondholders is spin-off execution: ADI separation will require debt allocation between entities, and the resulting leverage at each entity is undefined. The Products and Solutions stub may carry a disproportionate debt load relative to its smaller EBITDA, creating potential for a structurally leveraged outcome at the post-spin company.

Transocean is the world's largest offshore drilling contractor, operating a fleet of ultra-deepwater drillships and harsh-environment semi-submersibles. LTM financials: revenue $3.97B, EBITDA approximately $2.0B (FMP Q4 EBITDA $512M annualized, though LTM shows -$492M reflecting large non-cash impairments), FCF $626M. Capital structure is complex and substantial: ~$5.66B total debt, $997M cash, producing net debt of ~$4.66B. Total debt has declined ~$1.3B YoY through active deleveraging. The bond stack is multi-layered: $1.175B 8.75% Senior Secured Notes due Feb 2030 (5-rig collateral package), $687M 11.50% Senior Guaranteed Notes due Jan 2027, ~$248M residual 6.875% Senior Notes due Feb 2027, ~$22M residual 8.0% Senior Notes due Apr 2027, ~$609M 6.80% Senior Notes due Mar 2038, plus convertible 4.625% notes due Sep 2029. The $358M 8.375% 2028 secured notes were retired Mar 2026. A revolving credit facility (~$500M, maturity Jun 2028) is available. The credit question is whether Transocean's deleveraging trajectory (down $1.3B YoY) can continue fast enough to bring $5.7B total debt to a sustainable level before the deepwater cycle turns, or whether the massive debt legacy from the 2014-2020 downturn permanently constrains the credit regardless of the improved day rate environment. Bull catalyst: deepwater day rates sustained above $500k/day + contract backlog growth + continued deleveraging toward $4B debt. Bear catalyst: offshore capex pullback compressing day rates + $687M Jan 2027 maturity approaching without refi progress + impairment-driven losses eroding bondholder confidence. The 2027 maturity concentration ($687M + $248M + $22M = ~$957M) is the near-term wall.

RingCentral's credit profile is dominated by the near-term maturity of its $609M 2026 Convertible Notes (March 2026), creating acute refinancing risk against cash on hand of only $132M at year-end 2025. The company has $650M available under its term loan facility and $305M under its revolver -- providing theoretical firepower for the convert repayment -- but accessing this capacity would push gross leverage meaningfully higher from current 1.63x. Underlying business momentum is supportive: ARR grew to $2.67B (+7% YoY), FY25 total revenues were $2.5B, and management has delivered S&M leverage with SBC declining from 14% to 11% of revenue. GAAP operating income improved dramatically ($121M in FY25 vs $2.7M in FY24), confirming the earnings inflection. The 8.5% Senior Notes due August 2030 ($350M) reflect HY-adjacent credit pricing -- consistent with the liquidity risk and stockholders deficit position. The term loan ($302M, due 2030) has a reasonable amortization schedule ($15.5M/year) and interest rate swap reduces floating rate exposure. Post-convert refinancing, the 2030 debt wall ($350M + $302M residual) is manageable against $2.67B ARR. The pivotal near-term question is refinancing execution: can RNG retire the 2026 converts without materially increasing leverage?

Rockies Express Pipeline (REX) is a 1,679-mile interstate natural gas pipeline stretching from the Rockies (Opal, WY) to eastern Ohio, providing critical transportation capacity for both Rockies gas flowing east and, via bi-directional flow, Appalachian gas flowing west. REX is BBB-rated (IG) -- the highest-rated name in Gas Distribution coverage -- reflecting the FERC-regulated tariff structure that provides highly predictable, contracted revenue. The bond stack totals approximately $1.6B across four unsecured tranches: $550M 4.95% due Jul 2029, $400M 4.80% due May 2030, ~$325M 7.50% due Jul 2038, and ~$325M 6.875% due Apr 2040. The ~$150M unsecured RCF (Wells Fargo agent, accordion to $200M) provides modest liquidity. No FMP financial data is available -- REX is private and does not file SEC reports. Leverage and coverage metrics are available only from rating agency reports. The FERC-regulated tariff structure means revenue is largely insulated from commodity prices. The credit question is whether REX's contractual recontracting risk (as legacy long-term shipper contracts expire) will erode the revenue base, or whether the bi-directional capability and strategic position between Rockies and Appalachian supply basins maintain utilization. Bull catalyst: Appalachian gas production growth increasing east-to-west flows + FERC rate case supporting tariff increases. Bear catalyst: shipper contract expirations not renewed + competing pipeline capacity eroding REX's market position. The BBB rating and IG-level coupons (4.8-5.0%) distinguish REX from the rest of Gas Distribution coverage.
Limited public data available. Private credit — no SEC filings or market data for scoring.

RPM is a well-positioned IG specialty chemicals credit where the quantitative picture is clean — Debt/EV at ~19.5% is comfortably green, interest coverage at 10.4x (covenant-reported at 12.06x) provides massive headroom against the 3.50x minimum, and liquidity of $1.1B is strong — but the qualitative yellow flag is justified by the deliberate strategic pivot from cost optimization to debt-funded growth. The red on capital allocation reflects $600M+ in acquisition-related borrowings over the past year, an increasing capex trajectory ($220-240M guided), and simultaneous dividend/buyback expansion, all while the Consumer segment has been organically declining for 8+ quarters and tariff-driven input cost inflation is compressing gross margins 40-60bps. The 2027 revolver maturity ($562M drawn) is the nearest wall and drives the yellow maturity score; this needs to be refinanced within the next year, which should be straightforward given the credit profile but is worth monitoring if the M&A pace continues and leverage creeps up.

**Desk summary:** RPM's fundamentals are peer-leading and improving (green quant, positive momentum), but the composite gets pulled to yellow because management is explicitly redirecting MAP 2025 savings into M&A and growth capex rather than deleveraging — the $519M debt increase was absorbed without covenant stress (1.77x vs 3.75x limit), but the trajectory matters more than the snapshot. Watch the August 2027 revolver refi timeline alongside acquisition pace; if management executes another large deal before extending that facility, the maturity/leverage dynamic tightens meaningfully. The Consumer segment organic decline and tariff cost absorption are the near-term earnings risks that could narrow the covenant cushion if volumes don't stabilize — the 16% EBIT margin target is aspirational and back-end loaded, making the growth-over-deleveraging bet the key credit call on this name.

Range Resources is one of the premier Appalachian gas producers, operating exclusively in the Marcellus Shale in southwestern Pennsylvania with top-tier well economics and among the lowest all-in costs in US gas. LTM financials: revenue $2.99B, EBITDA $1.32B, FCF $1.02B -- exceptional free cash flow generation. Capital structure: $1.27B total debt ($1.21B long-term), near-zero cash, producing net debt of $1.27B and leverage of 1.0x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is strong at 12.6x on $105M LTM interest expense. The debt stack was reshaped in early 2026: the 8.25% 2029 notes (~$600M) were fully redeemed in Jan 2026, funded by ~$720M RBL draw. The remaining bond stack is approximately $500M 4.75% Senior Notes due 2030 plus other tranches totaling ~$1.1B. The $4.0B RBL facility ($3.0B borrowing base, $2.0B bank commitments) matures 2030 and had ~$720M drawn post-redemption. Near-term: the RBL draw needs to be repaid from FCF, which at $1B+ annual generation should occur within 2-3 quarters. No bond maturities before 2030. No maintenance covenants on the unsecured notes. The credit question is whether Range's exceptional Appalachian cost position (sub-$1.75/mcf full-cycle breakeven) and $1B+ FCF generation translate into a formal IG upgrade, or whether the aggressive 8.25% tender created a temporary RBL overhang that delays the upgrade timeline. Bull catalyst: RBL repaid within H1 2026 + formal IG upgrade from S&P/Moody's + sustained $3.50+ Henry Hub. Bear catalyst: sub-$2.50 gas for 12+ months compressing FCF + RBL utilization remaining elevated. Range is the strongest gas E&P credit after GPOR on pure leverage metrics, with the NGL kicker from the Martica complex adding revenue diversification.
Limited public data available. Private credit — no SEC filings or market data for scoring.

Seadrill Finance is the bond-issuing entity for Seadrill Limited (NYSE: SDRL), a premium deepwater and harsh-environment offshore driller operating a focused fleet of high-specification drillships and semi-submersibles. LTM financials: revenue $1.43B, EBITDA $260M (depressed by newbuild delivery timing and rig mobilization costs), FCF -$92M. Capital structure: ~$613M total debt ($575M 8.375% Senior Secured 2nd-Lien Notes due 2030 plus ~$50M unsecured convertible due Aug 2028), $339M cash, producing net debt of $274M and leverage of 1.1x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 4.3x on $61M LTM interest. The new revolving credit facility provides additional liquidity. Seadrill emerged from Chapter 11 in February 2022 with a clean balance sheet and has since focused on a lean, premium fleet strategy rather than the pre-bankruptcy mega-fleet model. The credit question is whether the premium fleet strategy generates enough EBITDA to support the $575M secured notes through a potential day rate normalization, or whether the lean fleet means revenue and EBITDA swing violently with individual rig contract renewals. Bull catalyst: harsh-environment contract wins (Norway, UK) at premium rates + EBITDA normalizing above $400M + full debt retirement path. Bear catalyst: rig contract gaps creating zero-revenue quarters + day rate mean reversion + newbuild delivery disruption. At 1.1x leverage, the credit is well-positioned but the volatile LTM EBITDA ($260M) creates coverage sensitivity.

SHW (Sherwin-Williams) — Desk Summary, April 2026

The quant-qual divergence here is real but manageable: quantitative scores are solidly green on the back of 12% Debt/EV, 9.6x interest coverage, strong liquidity ($3.6B undrawn revolver + $207M cash), and a peer-leading fundamental profile — but the maturity wall is the legitimate red flag, with ~$1.55B coming due in 2026 ($350M senior notes already refinanced into short-term borrowings plus $1.2B in CP/term loans), followed by a chunky $2.4B in 2027. Management is actively refinancing, but doing so at higher rates (~$85-90M incremental interest expense in 2026), which directly pressures cash coverage in a demand environment they themselves acknowledge is entering its third consecutive year of offering "not much help." The qualitative yellow is driven by the combination of elevated risk severity — particularly the unquantifiable lead paint litigation tail and debt that grew nearly $1B in 2025 for the Suvinil deal — alongside a capital allocation policy that still directs $2.5B annually to buybacks and dividends, explicitly limiting deleveraging speed even as the stated target is 2.0-2.5x (they're at 2.3x adjusted, 2.43x GAAP gross).

**What matters now:** Watch the 2026-2027 refinancing execution closely — roughly $3.95B needs to be termed out or rolled in the next 18 months, and the incremental carry cost is real against a backdrop of flat-to-down volumes and raw material headwinds from tariffs. Management tone is confident and pricing discipline appears intact, but the fundamental momentum is actually negative (-0.09), meaning SHW is deteriorating versus specialty chemical peers on a QoQ basis despite its strong absolute position. The lead paint litigation remains the unhedgeable left-tail risk; any adverse ruling could rapidly reprice a name that currently trades like a fortress credit. This is not a sell but it's a "watch the maturity wall and demand inflection" story — if 2026 volumes don't recover and refinancing costs continue climbing, the gap between green quant and yellow qual could close

SM Energy is a mid-cap E&P operating in the Permian Basin (Midland Basin) and, following the $4.5B Civitas/XCL acquisition (2024), the Uinta Basin in Utah. Production is approximately 207 MBoe/d (53% oil). LTM financials: revenue $3.15B, EBITDA $2.47B, operating cash flow $2.01B against LTM interest expense of $433M (elevated due to acquisition bridge financing). Capital structure: $2.30B total debt ($2.30B long-term), $368M cash, producing net debt of $1.93B and leverage of 0.8x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 5.7x -- adequate but below most Permian peers, reflecting the higher interest burden from acquisition debt. The debt stack is being actively reshaped: a $1.0B 6.625% Senior Notes due 2034 was issued in Mar 2026, proceeds funding the tender on $894M of the 8.375% 2028 Civitas legacy notes. The 6.75% 2026 notes (~$250M stub) and a $417M 2027 tranche are targeted for retirement in 2026. The $5.0B RBL ($2.5B committed, maturity extended to Jan 2031) is undrawn. No maintenance covenants on the unsecured notes. The credit question is whether SM can deleverage the post-Civitas capital structure fast enough while funding Uinta Basin development -- the Uinta adds waxy crude production that commands premium pricing but requires heavy upfront investment and new infrastructure. Bull catalyst: Uinta well results exceeding type curves + successful 2026 maturity cleanup + oil above $80 generating $500M+ FCF. Bear catalyst: Uinta execution challenges + oil below $55 compressing EBITDA below $1.5B + legacy Civitas debt overhang persisting. SM's post-acquisition cleanup mirrors CRGYFN's Vital integration, but at 0.8x leverage SM has more headroom.

South Bow Canadian Infrastructure is a crude oil pipeline company spun off from TC Energy in August 2024, operating the Keystone Pipeline System -- one of the most critical crude oil transportation arteries connecting the Western Canadian Sedimentary Basin to US Gulf Coast refineries. LTM financials: revenue $1.71B, EBITDA $885M, FCF $545M against $309M LTM interest expense. Capital structure is substantial: ~$5.78B total debt, $574M cash, producing net debt of $5.21B and leverage of 5.9x net debt/LTM EBITDA. Interest coverage is 2.9x. The bond stack was established via a massive $7.9B equivalent multi-tranche offering at spin-off, including CAD and USD tranches plus 7.625%/7.500% junior subordinated hybrid notes due 2055. A C$2.0B unsecured revolving credit facility was established Q3 2024. The nearest maturities are USD 4.911% 2027 and USD 5.026% 2029 tranches. The credit question is whether the Keystone system's contracted, FERC/CER-regulated tariff revenue can support the heavy 5.9x leverage inherited at spin-off, or whether the pipeline's age, regulatory risk, and environmental liability (prior Keystone spills) make the debt load too aggressive. Bull catalyst: WCSB production growth increasing Keystone throughput + leverage declining below 5x from EBITDA growth + TMX ramp reducing Canadian egress constraints and benefiting all pipeline operators. Bear catalyst: Keystone operational incident + FERC/CER tariff review cutting revenue + environmental liability accelerating + leverage remaining above 6x. The hybrid junior subordinated notes add structural complexity.

Saturn Oil & Gas is a Canadian light oil producer (TSX: SOIL) focused on the Viking and Cardium formations in Saskatchewan and Alberta, producing ~41-44k boepd (~81% oil). The company carries a unique capital structure: US$463M estimated outstanding of 9.625% Senior Unsecured Notes due Jun 2029 (originally US$650M, amortizing via mandatory quarterly prepayments of 10% p.a. of original principal at 104.813% call price). Saturn voluntarily repurchased ~$15M below par in Q1 2025, suggesting market pricing reflects some credit stress. Year-end 2025 net debt was approximately CAD$762M, with 2026 guidance targeting CAD$645-695M through continued amortization and FCF application. Leverage is guided at 1.4-1.7x net debt/EBITDA for YE2026 -- manageable for a single-B Canadian oil E&P. No separate RBL or revolver has been disclosed -- the notes are the primary debt instrument with the mandatory amortization acting as a built-in deleveraging mechanism. The 9.625% coupon is the highest in E&P coverage, reflecting the B1/B3 rating and Canadian single-name risk. Production guidance for 2026 is 39-41k boepd, slightly below Q4 2025 levels of 43.7k boepd, suggesting modest base decline. The credit question is whether the mandatory amortization schedule can bring leverage below 1.0x before the 2029 maturity, or whether a refinancing at lower rates is possible earlier. Bull catalyst: WCS pricing strengthening (TMX pipeline expansion improving Canadian egress) + voluntary buybacks below par continuing + production outperformance. Bear catalyst: WCS-WTI differential widening + CAD weakening increasing USD-denominated debt service burden + Viking/Cardium decline rates exceeding expectations. The mandatory amort structure provides a forced deleveraging that most HY E&P credits lack.

Superior Plus is a North American propane distribution company operating across Canada and the US, serving approximately 780,000 customer locations. The business is weather-dependent -- heating degree days drive residential propane demand, creating seasonal volatility. The bond stack includes US$600M 4.50% Senior Unsecured Notes due Mar 2029 (issued Mar 2021) and a CAD-denominated tranche (~C$ 4.25% due May 2028). A revolving credit facility provides operational liquidity. Superior is private with limited FMP data. The 4.50% coupon reflects the BB-rated credit quality and the low-rate 2021 issuance vintage. Propane distribution has a unique risk profile: weather-dependent demand, decentralized operations (hundreds of local distribution points), and customer switching risk from propane to electric heating. The credit question is whether the propane distribution model can sustain the debt load as electric heat pump adoption gradually erodes the residential propane market over the next decade, or whether the commercial/agricultural propane demand provides sufficient structural floor. Bull catalyst: cold winter driving above-normal heating demand + commercial/agricultural propane demand resilience + tuck-in acquisitions at reasonable multiples. Bear catalyst: mild winter collapsing residential demand + accelerating heat pump adoption + propane-to-electric switching in key markets. The weather sensitivity makes this the most seasonally volatile credit in energy coverage.
Limited public data available. Private credit — no SEC filings or market data for scoring.
